title: Memory Evolution — Memory Hierarchy and SOTA

notes.title: Von Neumann Architecture and the Memory Wall
notes.summary: Von Neumann architecture separates memory from the processing unit, creating a bottleneck because the PU executes instructions far faster than memory can be accessed.
notes.detail: The fetch-and-execute workflow fetches instructions and data from memory, executes them on the ALU, and writes results back to memory. This separation of memory and PU is the source of the Memory Wall.
keyPoints: Workflow: fetch from memory, execute on ALU, write back to memory
Separation of memory and PU creates the bottleneck
PU executes orders of magnitude faster than memory access

notes.title: Processor-DRAM Performance Gap
notes.summary: The performance gap between processors and DRAM grows about 50% per year, so faster processors alone do not guarantee faster applications.
notes.detail: The 50% gap describes the historical period shown in the graph. Faster processors alone do not guarantee faster applications.
keyPoints: Gap grows 50% per year
Describes the historical period in the graph
Faster processors alone do not guarantee faster applications

notes.title: Scaling Laws Meet Memory Walls
notes.summary: LLM scaling laws increase parameters, data, and context state, while post-Dennard scaling makes Tensor Core throughput grow much faster than HBM capacity, widening the memory wall.
notes.detail: LLM workloads increase the amount of parameters and data and increase chain-of-thought length and search depth, leading to larger model size and context state. Meanwhile Tensor Core throughput grows much faster than HBM capacity, widening the memory wall across generations.
keyPoints: LLM workloads: more parameters and data, longer chain-of-thought and search depth
Larger model size and context state
Tensor Core throughput outpaces HBM capacity, widening the wall across generations

notes.title: Memory Capacity per Core Gap
notes.summary: PU core count doubles every ~2 years while DRAM DIMM capacity doubles every ~3 years, so memory capacity per core is expected to drop by 30% every two years.
notes.detail: Because capacity per core shrinks, much data may load from low-speed disk.
keyPoints: Cores double every ~2 years; DIMM capacity every ~3 years
Capacity per core expected to drop 30% every two years
Much data may load from low-speed disk

notes.title: Memory Performance as the System Bottleneck
notes.summary: Bandwidth and latency trends worsen over time, making memory performance the typical bottleneck of modern computing systems.
notes.detail: The lecture presents trends showing that both memory bandwidth and latency have been worsening relative to processor demands. As a result, in modern computing systems memory performance is typically the bottleneck of the entire system, not just one component. This motivates the whole lecture: designing memory systems to fully utilize modern CPUs/GPUs, especially in the AI era.
keyPoints: Bandwidth and latency trends worsen over time
Memory performance is typically the bottleneck of entire systems
Motivates memory-system design for modern CPUs/GPUs in the AI era

notes.title: Registers and Caches Reduce Dependence on Main Memory
notes.summary: Registers and caches reduce how often execution depends on slower main memory, and data reuse near the processor reduces traffic across the hierarchy.
notes.detail: A high-level view of modern memory systems shows that registers and caches exist to reduce how often execution depends on slower main memory. Keeping reused data near the processor reduces traffic across the memory hierarchy. This is the organizing principle behind the deeper and larger cache hierarchies seen in real processors.
keyPoints: Registers and caches reduce dependence on slower main memory
Data reuse near the processor reduces hierarchy traffic
Explains why real chips invest die area in on-chip storage

notes.title: Deeper and Larger Cache Hierarchy
notes.summary: Modern systems use a deeper, larger cache hierarchy in which private caches keep frequently used data near each core and a shared cache supports reuse across the processor.
notes.detail: The AMD Barcelona (2007) example illustrates this structure.
keyPoints: Private caches keep frequently used data near each core
A shared cache supports reuse across the processor

notes.title: Cache Capacity Helps but Access Time Depends on Data Location
notes.summary: IBM POWER10 (2020) illustrates large shared caches: 15-16 cores, 2MB L2 per core, 120MB shared L3. Capacity reduces main-memory traffic, but access time still depends on where data resides.
notes.detail: The IBM POWER10 (2020) example has 15-16 cores, 2MB of L2 per core, and a 120MB shared L3. The lesson drawn is that cache capacity helps reduce traffic to main memory, while access time still depends on the location of the data in the hierarchy. Capacity and latency are therefore separate concerns when sizing caches.
keyPoints: POWER10: 15-16 cores, 2MB L2/core, 120MB shared L3
Cache capacity reduces traffic to main memory
Access time still depends on the location of the data

notes.title: GPU Cache Hierarchy: Per-SM L1 and Shared Device-Wide L2
notes.summary: Nvidia Ampere (GA102, 2020) has 128KB L1 per SM and 6MB shared L2; the A100 shares the architecture but adds more SMs and L2 caches. Many SMs share the device-wide L2.
notes.detail: The Nvidia Ampere GA102 (2020) provides 128KB of L1 per SM and a 6MB shared L2. The A100 accelerator shares the same architecture but includes more SMs and more L2 caches. Many SMs share the device-wide L2 cache, and a larger accelerator needs more capacity and data supply to keep its execution resources fed.
keyPoints: GA102: 128KB L1 per SM, 6MB shared L2
A100 shares architecture with more SMs and L2 caches
Many SMs share the device-wide L2
Larger accelerators need more capacity and data supply

notes.title: Stacked Cache Dies: AMD 3D V-Cache
notes.summary: AMD increased the L3 of its 8-core Zen 3 processors from 32MB to 96MB by stacking an additional 64MB L3 cache die on top of the processor die.
notes.detail: AMD increased the L3 size of its 8-core Zen 3 processors from 32MB to 96MB. The additional 64MB L3 cache die is stacked on top of the processor die, giving a total of 96MB of L3 cache. This shows cache capacity being scaled by 3D stacking rather than by enlarging the base die.
keyPoints: Zen 3 8-core L3 grows from 32MB to 96MB
Extra 64MB L3 cache die stacked on top of the processor die
Total of 96MB L3 cache

notes.title: Balancing Capacity, Access Time, and Reuse Across Storage Levels
notes.summary: The Apple M1 Ultra system (2022) places multiple storage levels around its compute resources, balancing capacity, access time, and reuse.
notes.detail: The Apple M1 Ultra System (2022) is used as an example of a system that places multiple storage levels around its compute resources. The design balances three competing goals: capacity, access time, and reuse. This summarizes the high-level design philosophy of modern memory systems.
keyPoints: Multiple storage levels surround the compute resources
Design balances capacity, access time, and reuse
Illustrated by Apple M1 Ultra (2022)

notes.title: Memory Hierarchy Principle
notes.summary: The memory hierarchy puts frequent data in fast, expensive, small memory and infrequent data in slow, cheap, large memory, and it works when a small active subset receives most accesses.
notes.detail: The working set changes over time. The hierarchy is useful when a small, active subset receives most accesses.
keyPoints: Frequent data: fast, expensive, small memory (e.g., cache)
Infrequent data: slow, cheap, large memory (e.g., main memory, disk)
Useful when a small active subset receives most accesses

notes.title: Locality in Practice: Loop and Array Access Patterns
notes.summary: A concrete code example shows how loops create temporal locality and array accesses create spatial locality, motivating cache-line fetches.
notes.detail: In the loop `for (i=0;i<100;i++) C[i]=A[i]*B[i]+D;`, the scalar D is reused every iteration, exhibiting temporal locality. The arrays A, B, and C are accessed in sequence, exhibiting spatial locality. Because neighboring elements are used together, the cache fetches an entire cache line in one transaction (e.g., C[0]..C[7]) rather than individual words, so subsequent accesses hit in cache.
keyPoints: Scalar reused across iterations = temporal locality
Sequential array access = spatial locality
Cache line fetched once serves multiple neighboring accesses
Exploiting locality reduces effective memory latency

notes.title: Cache Hit and Miss
notes.summary: A hit means the requested block is found in the current cache level with a valid tag match; a miss means it is absent and must be retrieved from the next lower level.
notes.detail: Hit rate is hits divided by total accesses, and miss rate is 1 minus hit rate. On a cache read/write, the data is found on the cache and then the read is performed.
keyPoints: Hit: block found with a valid tag match
Miss: block absent, retrieved from the next lower level
Miss rate = 1 - hit rate

notes.title: Average Memory Access Time (AMAT)
notes.summary: AMAT combines hit time with the miss rate times the miss penalty, and a cache helps only when common hits stay fast and few accesses pay the miss penalty.
notes.detail: The miss penalty is the time to fetch a block from a lower memory level, computed as access time plus data size divided by bandwidth. Access time is the latency for the memory to handle one access, while transfer time is the latency to transfer the data block to the higher level.
keyPoints: Miss penalty = access time + data size / bandwidth.
A cache helps when common hits remain fast and sufficiently few accesses pay the miss penalty.
notes.formula: \(AMAT = Hit\ time + Miss\ rate \times Miss\ penalty\)

notes.title: AMAT Worked Example and Improvement Levers
notes.summary: A numeric example computes AMAT for a first-level cache with 1-cycle hit, 10% miss rate, and 300-cycle DRAM penalty, then asks how to improve it.
notes.detail: AMAT = Hit Time + Miss rate × Miss Penalty. With hit time 1 cycle, miss rate 0.1, and miss penalty 300 cycles, AMAT = 1 + 0.1×300 = 31 cycles. The example frames the question of improvement: reducing miss rate (better locality, larger caches), reducing miss penalty (multi-level caches), or reducing hit time all lower AMAT.
keyPoints: AMAT = Hit Time + Miss rate × Miss Penalty
Example: 1 + 0.1×300 = 31 cycles
Improve by cutting hit time, miss rate, or miss penalty
Multi-level caches reduce effective miss penalty
notes.formula: AMAT = Hit Time + Miss rate * Miss Penalty

notes.title: Multi-Level Caches
notes.summary: Multi-level caches reduce the miss penalty by placing progressively larger, slower levels (L1, L2, L3) between the CPU and main memory (DRAM).
notes.detail: The page shows a hierarchy with approximate latencies of 1 clk for the first-level cache, 10 clks, 20 clks, and 300 clks for main memory, with second- and third-level caches in between.
keyPoints: Levels shown: L1, L2, L3, then main memory (DRAM).
Latencies increase from about 1 clk at L1 to about 300 clks at DRAM.

notes.title: Code Optimization: Blocking/Tiling
notes.summary: Blocking or tiling improves locality by processing data in small tiles instead of traversing it column-wise, which has poor locality.
notes.detail: The poor-locality example loops over columns then rows (sum += A[i][j]); the better version iterates over blocks of size B and calls compute_tile on each B-by-B submatrix.
keyPoints: Column-wise traversal gives poor locality.
Blocking/tiling gives better locality by computing on B-by-B tiles.

notes.title: End-to-End Load/Store Path: TLB, Cache, DRAM
notes.summary: A load/store goes through address resolution, the TLB, and the cache hierarchy, and only a miss through the caches sends the request to the memory controller and DRAM.
notes.detail: A TLB miss requires address translation work, while a cache miss determines whether the data must come from a lower level. Only a miss through the cache hierarchy sends the data request to the memory controller and DRAM.
keyPoints: A TLB miss requires address translation work.
Only a cache-hierarchy miss reaches the memory controller and DRAM.

notes.title: SRAM vs. DRAM
notes.summary: The page describes SRAM cell write and read operations, contrasting static storage with DRAM behind the cache.
notes.detail: A write drives the bit lines (bit=1, bitbar=0) and selects the row; a read precharges bit and bitbar to Vdd, selects the row, lets the cell pull one line, and the sense amp on the column detects the difference between bit and bitbar.
keyPoints: Write: drive bit lines and select the row.
Read: precharge to Vdd, select row, sense amp detects the bit/bitbar difference.

notes.title: DRAM Cell Operation: Read, Write, and Sense Amplification
notes.summary: Describes how a DRAM bit is written and read via bit lines and row selection, with sense amplifiers detecting tiny charge differences.
notes.detail: Write: drive the bit lines and select the row to store the value. Read: precharge the bit line to Vdd, then select the row so the cell and bit line share charge, producing a very small voltage change on the bit line. A sense amplifier detects changes of roughly 10–100k electrons, and the read is destructive so the value must be written back (restored).
keyPoints: Write drives bit lines and selects row
Read precharges bit line then shares charge with cell
Voltage change is very small; sense amp detects ~10–100k electrons
Read is destructive and requires restore

notes.title: DRAM Refresh
notes.summary: DRAM uses leaky storage and must be periodically refreshed across all rows, making each row un-accessible while it is refreshed.
notes.detail: With 4K rows and a 100ns read cycle, refreshing once takes 4096*100ns = 410µs; over a 64ms window this gives 410µs / 64ms = 0.64% unavailability.
keyPoints: 4K rows at 100ns per row gives 410µs to refresh once.
Refreshing causes 0.64% unavailability (410µs / 64ms).
Each row is un-accessible when refreshing.

notes.title: Why DRAM is Slow
notes.summary: DRAM is slow because of weak storage signals, slow sensing, destructive reads, and large dense arrays.
notes.detail: DRAM stores bits as tiny capacitor charges producing only a small voltage difference on long bitlines, and the sense amplifier must detect and amplify a very small voltage change into a full 0/1 value. Reading disturbs the stored charge so data must be restored after every row activation, and capacity-oriented arrays have long rows and bitlines.
keyPoints: Weak storage signal: tiny capacitor charges on long bitlines.
Sensing takes time: the sense amp amplifies a very small voltage change.
Destructive read: data must be restored after every row activation.

notes.title: Multi-Bank DRAM
notes.summary: Multi-banked DRAM chips provide independent storage arrays so work in one bank can overlap preparation in another, though the shared data bus still limits channel throughput.
notes.detail: Banks provide independent storage arrays, allowing work in one bank to overlap preparation in another. The shared data bus still limits how much data the channel can return at once.
keyPoints: Banks are independent storage arrays.
Work in one bank can overlap preparation in another.
The shared data bus limits how much data the channel returns at once.

notes.title: Multi-Bank, Multi-Rank DIMM
notes.summary: A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width, and multiple ranks share the channel while the controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.
notes.detail: A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width, and multiple ranks share the channel. The controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.
keyPoints: A rank combines DRAM chips into the channel data width.
Multiple ranks share the channel.
The controller selects a rank and schedules requests across its banks.

notes.title: Memory Controller Buffering and Scheduling
notes.summary: The memory controller buffers cache lines in both directions and schedules requests in two levels, bank and channel.
notes.detail: It holds a cache line read buffer and a cache line write buffer in both directions. Scheduling of requests is done in two levels: bank and channel.
keyPoints: Buffers cache lines in both directions (read buffer and write buffer).
Schedules requests in two levels: bank and channel.

notes.title: Channels and Channel Bandwidth
notes.summary: One memory-controller port drives one channel, where command, address, and clock signals select the destination and all ranks share the data bus.
notes.detail: Command, address, and clock signals select the destination, and all ranks share the data bus so only the selected rank may drive it. Peak bandwidth equals transfer rate times bus width divided by 8.
keyPoints: One memory-controller port drives one channel.
All ranks share the data bus; only the selected rank may drive it.
Peak bandwidth = transfer rate x bus width / 8.

notes.title: Channel Bandwidth Growth Axes and DDR5 Subchannels
notes.summary: Explains that channel bandwidth grows along three axes, that independent channels and bank scheduling raise utilization, and that DDR5's 32-bit subchannel split does not by itself double data width.
notes.detail: Bandwidth improves along three axes (implied: more channels, faster signaling, and wider/more efficient transfers). Independent channels add bandwidth when requests use them concurrently, and bank scheduling improves bus utilization. DDR5 splits the 64 data bits into two 32-bit subchannels; this split alone does not double total data width, so the benefit comes from concurrency and scheduling rather than raw width.
keyPoints: Independent channels add bandwidth under concurrent requests
Bank scheduling improves bus utilization
DDR5 splits 64 bits into two 32-bit subchannels
Subchannel split alone does not double total data width

notes.title: DDR1 to DDR5 Evolution
notes.summary: At the selected upper rates, the same aggregate x64 width rises from 3.2 to 51.2 GB/s across DDR1 through DDR5.
notes.detail: Throughput gains come from faster interfaces, longer bursts, and more bank parallelism, while cell access itself improves more slowly.
keyPoints: Aggregate x64 bandwidth grows from 3.2 GB/s to 51.2 GB/s at upper rates.
Faster interfaces, longer bursts, and bank parallelism raise throughput.
DRAM cell access improves more slowly than the interface.

topics.title: GPU Memory Hierarchy and Access Patterns

notes.title: GPU Memory Spaces and Access Times
notes.summary: The GPU hierarchy trades capacity for access time: registers, shared memory plus L1, L2, then off-chip GDDR/HBM device memory.
notes.detail: Registers are allocated per thread and hardware managed, shared memory plus L1 is a per-SM explicit scratchpad and hardware cache, and L2 is device-wide across all SMs. Device memory is off-chip physical memory serving the global address space.
keyPoints: Registers: per-thread, hardware managed.
Shared memory + L1: per-SM scratchpad and cache.
L2 is device-wide; GDDR/HBM is off-chip device memory.

notes.title: GPU Request Path: SM-Local Storage, L2, and Device DRAM
notes.summary: Traces a GPU memory access from SM-local storage through the on-chip interconnect to shared L2 and then to memory controllers and DRAM.
notes.detail: A request reaches the device-wide L2 through the on-chip interconnect; an L2 miss continues to a memory controller. All SMs share L2 and the DRAM partitions, which are implemented with GDDR devices or HBM channels. This shared structure explains why L2 and DRAM are contention points across SMs.
keyPoints: Request path: SM-local storage → interconnect → L2 → memory controller → DRAM
L2 miss proceeds to a memory controller
All SMs share L2 and DRAM partitions
DRAM partitions use GDDR devices or HBM channels

notes.title: Programmer's View of CUDA Memories
notes.summary: CUDA memory spaces are characterized by scope (which threads can access data) and lifetime (how long data exists).
notes.detail: __syncthreads() coordinates threads within one block only; it does not synchronize different blocks.
keyPoints: Scope identifies which threads can access the data.
Lifetime identifies how long the data exists.
__syncthreads() synchronizes within one block, not across blocks.

notes.title: CUDA Memory Space to Physical Resource Mapping
notes.summary: Every CUDA memory space maps to a physical resource, and local memory is thread-private in scope but usually resides in device DRAM.
notes.detail: Local memory passes through L1/L2. Register and shared-memory allocations limit how many blocks and warps can reside on an SM.
keyPoints: Local memory is thread-private but usually lives in device DRAM via L1/L2.
Register and shared-memory allocations cap resident blocks and warps per SM.

notes.title: Warp Memory Access and Coalescing
notes.summary: One warp memory instruction generates up to 32 addresses, which the coalescer groups by cache-sector or transaction granularity before DRAM access.
notes.detail: The resulting transaction count depends on alignment, address spacing, access width, and GPU architecture.
keyPoints: A warp memory instruction can produce up to 32 addresses.
The coalescer groups addresses by cache-sector or transaction granularity.
Transaction count depends on alignment, spacing, access width, and architecture.

notes.title: Coalescing into Fewer Transactions
notes.summary: Coalescing is evaluated per warp memory instruction; aligned, contiguous addresses touch fewer segments than misaligned or strided ones.
notes.detail: Misalignment can cross extra boundaries, while strided accesses can touch many more segments.
keyPoints: Coalescing is evaluated for one warp memory instruction.
Aligned, contiguous addresses touch fewer segments.
Misalignment crosses extra boundaries; strided access touches many more segments.

notes.title: Data Layout and Useful Bandwidth
notes.summary: Data layout determines useful memory bandwidth: row-wise and column-wise traversal can do the same arithmetic while transferring different byte counts.
notes.detail: Useful bandwidth depends on requested bytes relative to the bytes actually transferred.
keyPoints: Row-wise and column-wise traversal perform the same arithmetic but transfer different byte counts.
Useful bandwidth is requested bytes relative to bytes actually transferred.

notes.title: Shared Memory as Explicit On-Chip Stage
notes.summary: Shared memory is an explicit on-chip data stage where software chooses what to stage and when threads synchronize.
notes.detail: One off-chip load can support repeated on-chip reuse, reducing DRAM traffic and increasing arithmetic intensity.
keyPoints: Software explicitly chooses the data to stage and the synchronization points.
One off-chip load can feed repeated on-chip reuse.
Reuse reduces DRAM traffic and raises arithmetic intensity.

notes.title: Shared Memory Bank Conflicts
notes.summary: Bank conflicts serialize otherwise parallel shared-memory accesses; typical GPUs use 32 banks, and same-address reads can use broadcast.
notes.detail: Different addresses in the same bank require multiple service rounds, which differs from global-memory coalescing.
keyPoints: Typical GPUs use 32 banks (figure shows 8 for readability).
Same-address reads can use broadcast.
Different addresses in the same bank need multiple service rounds, unlike coalescing.

notes.title: From DDR DIMMs to GDDR
notes.summary: GDDR replaces socketed DIMMs with soldered devices and short point-to-point links, enabling higher per-pin data rates with less expandability.
notes.detail: DIMMs use multiple ranks, replaceable modules, and longer routed channels, whereas GDDR uses short, fixed point-to-point routes.
keyPoints: DIMMs: multiple ranks, replaceable modules, longer routed channel.
GDDR: soldered devices with short point-to-point links.
Short fixed routes permit higher per-pin rates but less expandability.

notes.title: GDDR Channels and Faster Signaling
notes.summary: Aggregate bandwidth is the sum across independent memory-controller channels, raised by more channels, wider buses, and faster signaling.
notes.detail: These same levers also raise pin count, routing complexity, and I/O power.
keyPoints: Aggregate bandwidth sums across independent memory-controller channels.
More channels, wider buses, and faster signaling raise pin count, routing complexity, and I/O power.

notes.title: GDDR5 to GDDR7
notes.summary: GDDR6X uses PAM4 as a vendor extension, while GDDR7 uses PAM3 and further divides the channels.
notes.detail: The rates shown are representative; actual rates depend on the product and speed bin.
keyPoints: GDDR6X: PAM4 as a vendor extension.
GDDR7: PAM3 with further channel division.
Shown rates are representative; actual rates depend on product and speed bin.

notes.title: HBM Wide Interfaces
notes.summary: HBM1–HBM3 use a 1024-bit interface per stack, while HBM4 expands the interface to 2048 bits, giving HBM its very wide channel organization.
notes.detail: Dense, short wiring improves bandwidth and energy per bit, but it requires advanced packaging.
keyPoints: HBM1–HBM3: 1024-bit interface per stack
HBM4: 2048-bit interface per stack
Wide, short wiring raises bandwidth and lowers energy per bit at the cost of advanced packaging

notes.title: HBM Stacked Memory Overview
notes.summary: An HBM memory stack places multiple dies in one package, connected by micro-bumps between adjacent dies and by TSVs that carry signals and power through the stack.
notes.detail: More stacked dies increase capacity, while a wide channel organization increases bandwidth.
keyPoints: Micro-bumps connect adjacent dies
TSVs carry signals and power through the stack
More stacked dies raise capacity; wide channels raise bandwidth

notes.title: 2.5D Packaging with Interposer
notes.summary: HBM commonly sits beside the XPU on an interposer, forming a 2.5D package with dense connections.
notes.detail: Dense connections improve bandwidth and energy per bit, with costs in assembly, yield, cooling, and power delivery.
keyPoints: HBM is placed beside the XPU on an interposer
Dense connections improve bandwidth and energy per bit
Costs fall in assembly, yield, cooling, and power delivery

notes.title: HBM1 to HBM4 Scaling
notes.summary: HBM scales through faster signaling, greater stack height, and the wider HBM4 interface.
notes.detail: Package space, thermal limits, and yield constrain stack count and height; per-stack figures are representative.
keyPoints: Three scaling levers: faster signaling, taller stacks, wider HBM4 interface
Package space, thermal limits, and yield limit stack count and height
Per-stack figures are representative, not fixed

notes.title: DDR vs. GDDR vs. HBM Trade-offs
notes.summary: DDR, GDDR, and HBM each optimize different constraints, so the right choice depends on the workload and system constraints.
notes.detail: DDR favors capacity, expandability, and cost per GB; GDDR balances pin bandwidth and board cost; HBM favors bandwidth per package and per watt.
keyPoints: DDR: capacity, expandability, cost per GB
GDDR: balance of pin bandwidth and board cost
HBM: bandwidth per package and per watt

notes.title: Banked Shared LLC
notes.summary: A banked LLC is logically shared but physically distributed, with a physical-address hash selecting a home LLC slice.
notes.detail: Reads and writes to remote slices would slow down memory access speed.
keyPoints: Logically shared, physically distributed
Physical-address hash selects the home LLC slice
Remote-slice reads/writes would slow memory access

notes.title: Cache Coherence and Write Propagation
notes.summary: Coherence is needed because a write can make another core's copy stale; it requires write propagation and write serialization.
notes.detail: Write propagation means other processors must eventually observe the write; write serialization means all processors must agree on one order for writes to the same location.
keyPoints: A write can make another core's copy stale
Write propagation: others must eventually observe the write
Write serialization: all processors agree on one order of writes to a location

notes.title: Snooping and Directory Coherence Protocols
notes.summary: Snooping broadcasts coherence requests, while a directory tracks owners and sharers to target the messages.
notes.detail: MESI describes permissions; snooping and directory designs determine how coherence messages reach the caches.
keyPoints: Snooping: broadcast coherence requests
Directory: track owners and sharers to target messages
MESI describes permissions, not message delivery

notes.title: Capacity Wall of LLM Inference (KV-Cache)
notes.summary: A DeepSeek case study shows the KV-cache capacity wall: a GB200 GPU offers roughly 150GB of HBM capacity for KV-cache, which is stressed at 1M context length.
notes.detail: The page compares approximate session KV-cache sizes for DeepSeek v3.2 and DeepSeek v4 (with CSA/HCA/SWA) against the given GB200 specification.
keyPoints: Available HBM capacity for KV-cache: ~150GB on GB200
KV-cache size grows with context length
DeepSeek v4 uses CSA/HCA/SWA; v3.2 is the comparison point

notes.title: Memory Extension with CXL
notes.summary: CXL extends memory through a unified host address map spanning host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM.
notes.detail: Software sees host-memory ranges, while hardware translates load/store instructions into CXL remote memory accesses.
keyPoints: Unified address map across host DRAM/HBM and CXL HDM
Software sees host-memory ranges
Hardware translates loads/stores into CXL remote accesses

notes.title: CXL Switches: Expansion, Pooling, Sharing
notes.summary: CXL switches enable expansion, pooling, and sharing of memory across hosts.
notes.detail: Expansion adds capacity to one host, pooling assigns portions of memory devices to different hosts, and CXL 3.0 coherent sharing differs from merely allowing several hosts to map the same memory region.
keyPoints: Expansion: add capacity to one host
Pooling: assign portions of memory devices to different hosts
CXL 3.0 coherent sharing is more than mapping the same region

notes.title: LPDDR Memory Extension
notes.summary: LPDDR extends the capacity an accelerator can address: Hopper keeps local HBM, while Grace connects LPDDR5X through the coherent NVLink-C2C CPU–GPU link.
notes.detail: LPDDR does not enlarge HBM itself; it extends the addressable capacity.
keyPoints: Hopper retains local HBM
Grace connects LPDDR5X via coherent NVLink-C2C
LPDDR extends addressable capacity, not HBM size

notes.title: Tiered Memory Management
notes.summary: Tiered memory management decides which data stays in HBM, keeping hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data there and placing large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier.
notes.detail: Promotion of data into HBM helps only when future reuse saves more than the transfer and bookkeeping cost.
keyPoints: Keep hot, latency-critical, frequently reused data in HBM.
Place large, cold objects in the LPDDR capacity tier.
Promotion pays off only if future reuse exceeds transfer and bookkeeping cost.

sources.35:
CPU Memory Hierarchy

DRAM Behind Cache: Why DRAM is Slow?
  Weak storage signal
 DRAM stores bits as tiny capacitor charges, producing only a small voltage
  difference on long bitlines.
  Sensing takes time
  The sense amplifier must detect and amplify a very small voltage change
   into a full 0/1 value.
  Destructive read
  Reading a DRAM cell disturbs its stored charge, so the data must be
  restored after every row activation.
  Large dense arrays
 DRAM prioritizes capacity and cost per bit, so rows/bitlines are long and
  have higher RC delay.
  Solution: Multi-Bank, Multi-Rank DRAM
